analysis.title: 73% Odds Of Another Puke: BTIG Says Today's Bounce Is A Coin-Toss, Not A "Fat Pitch"
key_insights: BTIG's Jonathan Krinsky says last week's selloff produced the first NYSE 80% downside volume day in nearly a year, ending what he calls the longest streak in at least 30 years. The Nasdaq 100 closed 4.8% below its 200DMA, the Philly semi index fell 12% on the week, and the S&P had its worst week since April 2025.

Since 1996 there are 15 prior cases of a first 80% NYSE downside day in at least three months. In 11 of them at least one more 80% day followed within 30 trading days, and a third of the time there were five or more. This implies roughly a 73% chance of another one in the next month.

Forward S&P returns after such a first 80% day are negative at 5 and 10 days on average and median. At 20 days the SPX was higher only 53% of the time, with a +0.31% average return. Krinsky calls it a coin-toss for 20-50 day returns.

Historical analogs in the table: January 2018 was followed by five more 80% days, January 2020 by nine and a 32% drawdown 40 days out, and March 2025 by five more and a 9% drop within a week. December 2024 and October 2025 had zero and one follow-up and drifted higher.

Today's rebound (Nov 10) was broad: Goldman's desk counted more than 420 S&P names higher by midday, in line with the broadest rallies this year. The S&P was up over 2.5%, the Nasdaq 100 up 3.5%, the SOX up 5% and the VIX down more than 5 points to 20, even as Nvidia fell 6% on a report about Jensen Huang.

Goldman's desk describes the rally as light-activity: volume tracked 14% below the five-day average, versus last Thursday's session at 1.5x the 50-day average. Goldman flows were only 3% better to buy, with hedge funds and long-onlies marginally net buyers. The desk reads the move as a lack of supply more than buyside chasing.

Goldman noted a second straight day of buy skew in semis ex-NVDA ('at minimum, the intense selling has stopped'). Its prime brokerage flagged that last week's global tech selling matched the largest week on record. CTAs have been selling a lot of S&P, and Goldman models show another $25B or more of potential CTA supply this week.

The levered semi ETFs SOXL and SOXS both set record volume days last week. Goldman's Lee Coppersmith highlighted that realized volatility of the VVIX hit an all-time high on both 5-day and 10-day bases.

Krinsky says touching the 200DMA (about 7,325 on the S&P per BTIG, 7,328 per Goldman, which held) is not a fat pitch. A break lower toward 7,000-7,100 on SPX, with a bigger breadth washout, would be a fat-pitch setup. The S&P was around 7,546 at noon, so that level is roughly 6-7% lower.

Breadth is not washed out: 58% of S&P names are still above their 200DMA, versus under 30% at the April 2025 low. 20-day put/call ratios remain well below the levels seen at the March and July SPX lows.

QQQ has broken below its 200DMA and July lows, with next support around $635 from the late-2025 and early-2026 highs. Goldman says NDX was still a touch below its 200DMA at the day's highs. Bloomberg notes breaks of more than 3% have historically taken about 25 trading days to reclaim.

The SOX closed below its 200DMA for the first time since May 2025. Prior first cracks saw strong bounces but 50-day returns were negative. Krinsky says purchases from May to October are underwater, giving six months of overhead supply. He sees a move back to the April breakout around 8,000-8,300 as necessary, versus 9,390 on Friday, which is 12-15% lower.

Krinsky sees tactical downside in the stocks that held up. XLV hit an all-time high Thursday and was nearly 20% above its 200DMA, the widest spread on record, and he calls it a fat pitch on the short side. AAPL 'loses two ways' because it was a hideout during the semi/AI unwind: it is sold if risk-off deepens and rotated out of if semis bounce.

Other high-quality names are vulnerable to a near-term unwind. Longer term Krinsky sees high vs. low quality bottoming at the 2000 lows after a six-year bear market, and the Morgan Stanley Quality Short basket is rolling over below its 200DMA.

GDX is breaking a downtrend even with spot gold near YTD lows. Krinsky is still not a fan of precious metals but notes commodity stocks sometimes lead the commodity. RGLD is his quality setup in the group.

Bull counterpoints: JPMorgan's Dubravko Lakos-Bujas sees the selloff as nearly exhausted, calls it a deleveraging event and keeps an 8,000 year-end target. Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson also thinks the correction is nearing its end. Goldman notes buybacks are back. CPI is due tomorrow (Nov 11).

tension_points.bull_case: JPMorgan's Lakos-Bujas sees the selloff as nearly exhausted, a deleveraging event, with an 8,000 year-end target. Morgan Stanley's Wilson thinks the correction is nearing its end. Goldman notes buybacks are back, and the first 80% day is typically a necessary part of bottoming.
tension_points.bear_case: BTIG's Krinsky says a first 80% downside day is a coin-toss for 20-50 day returns, with about a 73% chance of another within 30 trading days. Breadth (58% above the 200DMA) and put/call ratios are not washed out, volume on the rebound is light, and CTAs may sell $25B or more this week.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A move toward 7,000-7,100 on SPX with breadth under about 30% of names above the 200DMA would set up a fat pitch and mark the washout. On the other side, BTIG's bear case is weakened if no further 80% downside day arrives in the next 30 trading days.

tension_points.bear_case: Krinsky says the SOX is below its 200DMA with six months of overhead supply from May-October buyers, and 50-day returns after similar breaks are negative. He wants a retrace to 8,000-8,300.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Krinsky's bear case would be challenged by a reclaim of the SOX 200DMA, which is not given as a numeric level. A fall to 8,000-8,300 on the SOX would, in his view, complete the retrace.
